title: The Night Gampel Pavilion Opened
dek: Before a sellout crowd of 8,241, UConn opened its new on-campus arena by beating No. 15 St. John's 72-58 and moving into a tie for first in the Big East.

setup.text: For 36 years, UConn's home on campus was the Field House, which opened in 1954. The Huskies won 282 of 367 games there, and they closed it on Wednesday night, Jan. 24, 1990, by beating Central Connecticut 99-77.

Its replacement was the domed basketball arena of a new campus sports complex. The state provided $22 million, and Harry A. Gampel, a 1943 UConn graduate, gave $1 million — the largest private gift to the university at the time — and his name went on the building. Construction began in the summer of 1987, and the arena was finished three months early so UConn could fit five games into the season.

UConn had not played a Big East game on campus since Feb. 11, 1986; its conference home games had gone to the Hartford Civic Center or the New Haven Coliseum. Back-to-back wins over Syracuse and Georgetown in Hartford had just lifted the Huskies into the AP poll at No. 20, and they brought a six-game winning streak into opening night.
The opponent was No. 15 St. John's: 17-3, alone in first place in the Big East at 6-1, and a 93-62 winner over UConn on Jan. 2.

story.text: Outside before tipoff, a student hunting for a ticket was offered one for $150 and walked away. Inside, Gov. William O'Neill tossed up a ceremonial jump ball and was roundly booed when he was introduced.
The fans stayed on their feet until UConn scored its first points: Rod Sellers' layup, 2 minutes 11 seconds in, which tied it 2-2.

It was a grind. Calhoun said UConn couldn't press because St. John's Boo Harvey handled the ball so well, and Nadav Henefeld, Tate George and Sellers combined to shoot 3 for 22. Chris Smith kept the Huskies close with 15 first-half points, and Scott Burrell, in his second game back from arthroscopic knee surgery, scored 12 off the bench before halftime.

Smith's 3-pointer at the halftime buzzer made it 35-34. St. John's, which had shot 68.6 percent against UConn on Jan. 2, made only 8 of 30 shots after halftime; Malik Sealy still finished with 26 points and 13 rebounds, but Jayson Williams was held to 6 and Robert Werdann to 4.

sequence.text: Rod Sellers' layup, 2:11 into the game, is UConn's first basket in its new home and ties the score.
Chris Smith's 3-pointer at the buzzer, capping a 15-point half for him, puts UConn ahead at halftime.
Malik Sealy's jumper ties it. St. John's will not score again for more than five and a half minutes.
Dan Cyrulik, a 7-foot sophomore who came in averaging 5 points, gives UConn the lead with a turnaround jumper.
Henefeld, scoreless for the first 34 minutes, hits a fadeaway jumper from the baseline.
With just over five minutes left, Henefeld's steal — his 91st of the season, an NCAA record for a freshman — turns into a John Gwynn layup.
The 6-foot Gwynn slips inside among the big men and tips in a Henefeld miss.

Final: UConn 72, St. John's 58. After the 10-0 run that broke the 51-51 tie, St. John's never challenged again. The win was UConn's seventh straight and sixth straight in the Big East, and it pulled the Huskies even with St. John's for first place.

quotes.text: I think we'll keep this place for a while.
The scoreboard said we were up one, but mentally we were down by six.
We won the game; nothing else is important.

aftermath.text: The next AP poll put UConn at No. 13, the program's highest wire-service ranking up to that point.
Four nights later, the UConn women played their first game in the building, beating Georgetown 76-54 before a program-record crowd of 3,151.
The men went 5-0 in Gampel that winter. One of those wins came on Feb. 19, when Henefeld's 3-pointer from the top of the key with two seconds left beat Providence 75-72 in overtime.
UConn went on to share the Big East regular-season title, win the conference tournament and reach the Elite Eight, finishing 31-6.

legacy.text: Gampel's capacity grew to 10,027 before the 1996-97 season and to 10,167 in 2002-03; by 2015 UConn described it as the largest on-campus basketball arena in New England.
In February 2020, UConn marked the building's 30th anniversary at halftime of a game against Cincinnati by honoring the 1989-90 team, the first to play there.
